name: PRF (platelet-rich fibrin)

lead: PRF is made by spinning your own blood without anticoagulant so platelets and white cells are trapped in a fibrin clot. Forum users on looksmax.org try it for dark under-eye circles and eye bags, hoping for a lighter, fuller eye area, and it also appears as a component of clinic-made or DIY facial serums.

Activated platelets in the fibrin matrix release growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF and EGF, which are thought to support tissue quality. It is established in dental and oral surgery for socket preservation, sinus lifts and periodontal regeneration, while the published trials are dental and none examine under-eye appearance. User reports on dark circles are mixed.

paras: Blood is drawn and centrifuged immediately in a clinic, and the resulting clot layer is used as a material or processed into a serum or injectable. For the eye area it is a clinic-made or DIY approach rather than a standard protocol.
No controlled safety data exist for under-eye injection or homemade serums in the sources reviewed. PRF preparation falls under an FDA product code that is 510(k) exempt.

angle.text: Forum users try PRF, a fibrin clot made from their own blood, for dark under-eye circles and eye bags, hoping growth factors lighten and fill the area; reports are mixed. It is established in dental surgery, and no facial trials were found.

lead: Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), also called leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF), is a derivative of platelet-rich plasma in which a person's own platelets and white blood cells are held in a fibrin matrix. Blood is drawn without anticoagulant and centrifuged immediately, producing a clot layer between platelet-poor plasma and red cells. [1] A 2006 series of papers by Dohan, Choukroun and colleagues described it as a 'second-generation platelet concentrate'. [2][3][4]

PRF is used mainly in oral and maxillofacial surgery for socket preservation, sinus lifts, periodontal regeneration and regenerative endodontics. [1] In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an under-eye treatment for dark circles and eye bags, and as a component of DIY or clinic-made facial serums. [5][6][7] Published trials in the sources reviewed are dental; none examined under-eye appearance.
infobox: Dental and oral surgery tissue healing
FDA product code KST, 510(k) exempt blood-draw/hematology product

paras: Wikipedia describes PRF as differing from PRP by retaining leukocytes and forming a fibrin scaffold, and states that activated platelets release growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF and EGF. The article argues the fibrin matrix is central to its therapeutic potential. [1] A 2009 classification in Trends in Biotechnology sorted platelet concentrates into four categories by leukocyte and fibrin content, from pure PRP to leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin, noting that applications had been confusing because each method yields a different product. [8]

Human trials found in the sources are mostly dental: ridge preservation with L-PRF and A-PRF [9], sinus lift with PRF versus xenograft [10], periodontal pockets [11], tooth extraction sockets [12], third-molar surgery and facial swelling [13], regenerative endodontics [14], and thickening of thin gingival phenotype with injectable PRF [15][16]. The records reviewed list small sample sizes (10 to 60 participants) and do not themselves report outcomes.

Wikipedia cites a meta-analysis reporting better clinical and radiographic periodontal outcomes with PRF than open flap debridement alone, with results comparable to demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft. [1] The 2006 Dohan paper on tissue healing is the foundational clinical description. [4]
No study of PRF for dark circles or under-eye bags was found in the sources consulted.
